newsitem.title: USA: Mass. acting governor sees up to $400 mln surplus.
newsitem.headline: Mass. acting governor sees up to $400 mln surplus.

text.p: The acting governor of Massachusetts Paul Cellucci on Monday predicted the state would have as much as a $400 million surplus when it finally closes the books on the 1997 fiscal year.

Cellucci, who recently became acting governor after William Weld stepped down from the position to fight for his nomination as ambassador to Mexico, said this would be the windfall left after the legislature agreed on plans to spend another $200 million or so on one-time capital projects.

The acting governor said: "I think it (the surplus) could be anywhere from $300 million to $400 million, although I think the legislature is probably going to allocate some of the surplus revenue to one-time capital projects."

Cellucci made the forecast during an interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV), which was scheduled to be shown on Tuesday at 1130 EDT, along with an interview with the Massachusetts treasurer.
The acting governor later explained his forecast was smaller than one offered by the treasurer because that official did not appear to have deducted the legislature's extra capital spending.

Treasurer Joe Malone, who is competing against Cellucci in next year's Republican primary for governor, said he looked for the state's 1997 surplus to run from $600 million to $700 million. Massachusetts ended the 1997 fiscal year on June 30.

Both elected officials agreed that Massachusetts might see its strong economy, which leads New England, boost revenues again in the new fiscal year. "If the economy continues as strong as it is, I think we'll see a significant surplus again next year," said Cellucci.

His rival, the state treasurer, who also looked for the latest federal tax changes to stimulate growth, said: "My guess is that it'll be in the same range as we had this year, but I wouldn't suggest that anybody tied that down as a leadpipe prediction."

The acting governor said he expected the legislature to approve as soon as this week proposals to spend some of the surplus on a range of projects, from economic development, a category that includes a Basketball Hall of Fame, to environmental programs and work on at least one seaport.

Noting that using pay-as-you-go funding would take some of the pressure off the state's capital budget, he said: "It's not as good as a tax cut, but it's a lot better than building on the base of the operating budget."
